scope: First-principles production/evaluation component audit and retrospective evidence-availability diagnosis.

diagnosis.interpretation: Descriptive cases, not causal percentages or independent samples; includes repeated questions across profiles and an interrupted cohort.
conclusions: Retrieval absence does not explain every wrong answer: necessary code was delivered in twelve audited losses.
Missing code remains real: same-file selection loss and never-requested dependencies are distinct failure paths.
Production used fewer requests than native in the completed development cohort while consuming more tokens; excess turns are not that cohort explanation.
Catalog overhead is measured before source retrieval: production 1158/compact 513 extra initial input tokens versus native, same catalog retained in later requests.
Historical 22/24 versus 17/24 claims were localization proxy passes, not source-reviewed answer correctness; current documentation is corrected.
Component fixes and passing local tests do not establish improved final-answer accuracy or cumulative model-token cost.

workflow_evidence.scope: Completed development study only; fixed-question descriptive workflow audit.
findings: Production and compact used fewer API requests and tool calls than native @6, but more total tokens. Excess turn count is not the observed explanation for this completed cohort.
Matched initial requests isolate 1158 extra input tokens for production and 513 for compact against native, before any tool observation; all later requests retain the catalog.
Character overhead measures JSON serialization and metadata, not provider token attribution or API cost.
No tool catalog removal or retrieval improvement is simulated as a measured answer-quality gain.

intake.scope: file_discovery.py, index.py, tokenize.py, chunker.py, and all seven symbols Python modules
intake.method: Offline production-function smoke over temporary workspaces; installed Python AST and JavaScript/TypeScript/TSX/Rust parsers; real SQLite and Windows directory junctions. Socket connections are blocked in the smoke. No paid APIs, models, embedding downloads, frozen artifact edits, or benchmark-win claims.

source_origin.baseline: smoke_intake.py inserted checkout src at sys.path[0] from its first run; baseline preceded explicit origin recording

components.responsibility: Expand includes, enforce resolved workspace root, extension/hidden/size/static-exclude and root ignore filtering.
components.reachability: Default for discover/find_files/find_symbols/find_evidence and schema include expansion; explicit file entries also have schema-owned validation outside this slice.
components.implemented: Root .gitignore now overrides lower-priority .git/info/exclude; .mts and .cts enter default discovery, matching existing TypeScript providers. Docstring now accurately states nested ignore files are not loaded.
risks: Nested .gitignore is ignored.
Static node_modules/build patterns match root-level paths, not nested equivalents.
Default hidden/extension/200000-byte filters omit files even for explicit include patterns.
Escaping junction anywhere in broad discovery aborts the whole request rather than skipping that entry.

components.responsibility: Persistent per-workspace symbol extents and hashing-feature cache; graceful misses and write failures.
components.reachability: Default from find_symbols and find_evidence; not the select_context candidate cache.
components.implemented: Validate symbol row shape/field types/line bounds; reject malformed, text-typed, nonfinite, negative, duplicate-key or trailing feature data as misses; store float64 weights without precision loss; bump FORMAT to 4; close connection when open initialization fails. Existing caller signature imports FORMAT, invalidating old production rows.
risks: Size plus mtime_ns cannot detect content changes preserving both values; changing cache key would require cross-module contract work.
Float64 increases stored feature bytes; no performance or ranking-win claim was measured.
Process concurrency and permission ACL matrices were not exhaustively exercised.

components.responsibility: Default tiktoken o200k_base counting/encoding and approximate whitespace fallback.
components.reachability: Default in select/chunking/tracing/review; whitespace explicitly selectable and fallback only on ImportError.
components.implemented: Correct misleading docstrings: whitespace decoding does not preserve source whitespace; offline tiktoken use needs cached encoding data. No tokenizer behavior was silently changed.
risks: Whitespace fallback corrupts indentation/newlines in decode-based paths.
Installed tiktoken with an empty encoding cache fails offline rather than taking ImportError fallback.
Individual BPE token slices may decode to U+FFFD despite whole-text reversibility.

components.responsibility: Contiguous raw-text chunks, exact character slices, line-additive token coordinates; oversized lines remain intact.
components.reachability: Default select_context chunking and lower-level library callers.
components.implemented: Unchanged: ordinary raw reconstruction and character contiguity pass; changing line conventions only here would disagree with select/schema/search callers.
risks: str.splitlines counts formfeed and Unicode U+2028 as lines, while Python AST uses physical newlines.
Line-additive coordinates are not whole-file tokenizer coordinates: two newline characters are two additive tokens but one whole-file token.
A single line can exceed block_size by design and later fail a selection budget; chunker itself preserves it.

components.responsibility: Public symbol types/provider/candidate exports.
components.reachability: Default imported by select.py and symbol_search.py; legacy generator and batch convenience function remain public but are not called by production src or active eval Python harness sources.
evidence: smoke_intake.py imports and exercises the namespace
risks: Public legacy exports imply compatibility obligations; no destructive removal was made during audit.

components.responsibility: FileSymbols/SymbolDef contract, identifier splitting, line-additive offsets.
components.reachability: Default across candidates, tracing/review, select and search; offsets directly exercised against chunker.
risks: Shares splitlines/physical-line mismatch with chunker.
Identifier splitting is ASCII-oriented; it is not a language binding resolver.
Definition dependency sets have provider-specific precision and must not be presented as exact call graphs.

components.responsibility: Extension-to-language dispatch, lazy provider availability, exact-text parse memoization.
components.reachability: Default from select/search, provider lookup from trace/review; parse_symbols cache applies only callers using that wrapper.
risks: Unsupported languages have lexical retrieval but no symbol provider.
Provider unavailability is cached for process lifetime and surfaced as None; missing grammar and unsupported extension are not distinguished here.
2048 exact-text cache entries retain source text; memory behavior not measured.

components.responsibility: Stdlib AST extraction of definitions, module assignments, imports and approximate references.
components.reachability: Default Python provider, including .pyi; parser dependency is stdlib ast, not installed tree-sitter-python.
components.implemented: Convert AST UTF-8 byte columns to Python character offsets; build physical-newline offsets so formfeed/U+2028 do not truncate node text; include positional-only, variadic positional and variadic keyword parameters in defines rather than refs.
risks: Decorator source remains outside function extent although decorator identifiers enter refs.
Tuple assignment is named <assignment> with no declared binding names.
A syntax error anywhere and a leading UTF-8 BOM string both yield no Python symbols, even if earlier definitions are valid.
Exact provider text does not resolve downstream splitlines coordinate mismatch.

components.responsibility: Installed JavaScript, TypeScript, TSX and Rust tree-sitter extraction with byte-to-character conversion.
components.reachability: Default for supported non-Python symbol languages; grammar loading is lazy but dependencies are mandatory in pyproject.toml.
components.implemented: TypeScript and TSX type aliases are kind type; enums are kind enum, not function, making existing kind filters meaningful.
risks: TS/Rust parameter type names enter defines and disappear from refs.
Arrow-function parameters are refs rather than local defines.
Aliased JS/Rust import source and local names are both defines; Rust trait method declarations without bodies are not separate definitions.
Provider parse/availability broadly swallows errors; parsing success does not imply semantic binding correctness.
tree-sitter-python is installed and declared but unused by production Python extraction; dependency removal is a recommendation, not performed here.

components.responsibility: Score symbol definitions into line-additive candidates and deduplicate by source/token interval.
components.reachability: symbol_candidates is used by default selection; file_symbol_candidates is a public convenience wrapper without production/active harness callers.
components.implemented: Candidate text now covers its claimed complete lines, so same-line sibling statements are not lost when equal interval keys deduplicate.
risks: A definition over max_tokens is skipped entirely by this lane, not split; other chunk lanes may still retrieve it.
Same-line merged text retains the winning definition's metadata rather than a union of sibling metadata.
Physical parser line numbers still mismatch chunker's splitlines after formfeed/U+2028.

components.responsibility: Legacy Python-only token-window candidate generator using structural/lexical scores.
components.reachability: Public export and dedicated tests, but no production src or active eval harness caller located; frozen study copies remain unchanged.
components.implemented: Recommendation only: evaluate removal in an explicit public API migration. For the retained callable, reuse corrected AST character-bound conversion rather than leaving confirmed corruption.
evidence: grep source references limited to exports/tests/frozen copies/new smoke
risks: Duplicates current symbol lane with incompatible prefix-token coordinate semantics.
Arbitrary BPE token windows can cut Unicode bytes; whitespace tokenizer windows normalize source.
No public API removal was authorized or performed; it cannot be claimed to explain default PASR agent failures while unwired.

scenarios.observed: Root keep.py negation lost to .git/info/exclude before, preserved after. Rewriting root .gitignore immediately includes ignore.py and excludes keep.py on the next call. Git -z check-ignore confirms root and nested patterns; PASR still includes src/nested.py.

200000-byte text included; 200001-byte text excluded. Hidden files, Dockerfile and unknown.xyz excluded by defaults. .mts/.cts were provider-supported but undiscovered before and included after. Parent/absolute paths rejected. Actual Windows junction escape rejected for explicit, glob and broad includes. File-symlink creation fails with WinError 1314.

Binary-looking .py is discovered and delivered containing NUL/U+FFFD. Latin-1 bytes become U+FFFD. UTF-16 needle is read as replacement/NUL-separated text and not found, while ASCII needle in two other files is found. CRLF is normalized to LF before downstream retrieval.

Same-size alpha-to-bravo edit with changed mtime refreshes find_symbols. Same-size bravo-to-delta edit restoring identical mtime returns zero delta matches, while direct production parser sees delta. In-process parse_symbols exact-text cache separately returns old_name then new_name correctly.

Before, malformed valid JSON entries escaped validation, text BLOB raised TypeError, NaN/trailing bytes were accepted, f32 changed 0.1/1/3, and corrupt DB open leaked a Windows handle. After, malformed rows are misses, weights are exact, corrupt DB file unlinks immediately. Actual query_only write failure is swallowed and subsequent writes recover. Unusable cache directory does not prevent find_evidence returning source evidence.

Seven newline/blank/long-line cases reconstruct exactly. Two LF characters count as one whole-file token versus two additive tokens. Whitespace decode removes indentation/newlines; cached tiktoken whole-text roundtrip works; individual DNA emoji tokens each decode U+FFFD. A fresh subprocess with empty encoding cache and denied network exits 1 from get_tokenizer rather than falling back.

Before answer assignment was 'wer = "YES"; n' after preceding non-ASCII bytes. Both providers now return 'answer = "YES"'. Formfeed/U+2028 provider text is exact after correction. Positional-only/*args/**kwargs move to defines, away from refs. Decorators, tuple assignment, BOM and syntax-error limitations remain recorded.

All installed providers execute. JS Unicode source offsets remain exact. TS alias/enum kinds change from function to type/enum. Typed-parameter and alias-binding approximation remains. Same-line alpha/beta text changed from alpha-only to complete line. Large relevant definition produces zero symbol-lane candidates at 16 tokens. U+2028 candidate still selects wrong lines despite exact provider text.

findings.finding: AST byte columns were treated as Unicode string character columns, corrupting delivered symbol source slices.
findings.causal_relevance: Known local corruption mechanism. Hypothesis only for recorded agent failures; no recorded failing case was linked by this slice.
findings.disposition: fixed with behavioral regressions

findings.finding: Full-line candidate keys with node-only text allowed same-line deduplication to discard source evidence.
findings.reproducible_evidence: intake_before.json#/same_line_candidates contains alpha only; intake_after.json contains alpha and beta line.
findings.causal_relevance: Known local byte-loss mechanism before fusion. Recorded-case relevance unproven.
findings.disposition: fixed for same-line windows; separate newline-coordinate issue remains

findings.finding: Python physical lines and str.splitlines coordinate systems disagree on formfeed/U+2028. Candidate for target after a U+2028 string contains a previous string tail and omits return body.
findings.causal_relevance: Known local evidence substitution/loss. No evidence these control characters occurred in recorded failures.
findings.disposition: unresolved cross-component line convention; provider's own character slicing fixed, global cutover not attempted

findings.finding: Corrupt-cache fallback contract was violated by valid JSON with invalid fields, non-BLOB feature values and leaked failed-open SQLite handles.
findings.reproducible_evidence: intake_before.json#/index_corrupt_symbols; intake_before.json#/index_corrupt_blocks; intake_before.json#/index_corrupt_handle_released; matching after keys show misses/closed handle.
findings.causal_relevance: Known local exception/stale-metadata risk. No corrupted index was established in recorded agent failures.
findings.disposition: fixed; scoped smoke covers actual SQLite rows and failed open

findings.finding: float32 cache changed full-precision hashing weights despite cache-equivalence guarantee.
findings.reproducible_evidence: intake_before.json#/index_roundtrip exact_blocks false; after true for 0.1 and 1/3.
findings.causal_relevance: Known numerical mismatch. A ranking or answer difference was not established by intake smoke.
findings.disposition: fixed using float64 and FORMAT 4; no claimed benchmark improvement

findings.finding: Same-size edits preserving mtime return obsolete symbols from persistent cache.
findings.reproducible_evidence: intake_after.json#/cache_same_size_preserved_mtime has zero delta hits while direct parser sees delta.
findings.causal_relevance: Known local stale answer mechanism. Whether study workspaces were modified with preserved timestamps is unknown.
findings.disposition: documented limitation; content-identity cache contract requires measured cross-module redesign

findings.finding: Root ignore precedence excluded explicitly unignored files; supported .mts/.cts were filtered out before parsing.
findings.reproducible_evidence: intake_before.json#/discovery_initial versus intake_after.json#/discovery_initial; Git reference in after.
findings.causal_relevance: Known pre-retrieval omission. Recorded failures have not been matched to these filenames/extensions.
findings.disposition: fixed with default discovery regressions

findings.finding: Nested .gitignore files are not loaded; static build/vendor exclusion patterns do not exclude nested paths.
findings.reproducible_evidence: intake_after.json#/git_ignore_reference marks src/nested.py ignored; discovery_initial includes it plus src/build/output.py and src/node_modules/vendor.js.
findings.causal_relevance: Known extra-noise mechanism. Dilution of actual recorded rankings remains a hypothesis, not measured causation.
findings.disposition: documented/recommend hierarchical ignore semantics and explicit static-pattern scope decision; no speculative matcher rewrite

findings.finding: Extension/size filtering precedes decoding, but binary/encoding validation does not. UTF-8 replacement destroys non-UTF8 bytes and UTF-16 textual query matching; newline normalization changes bytes.
findings.reproducible_evidence: intake_after.json#/binary_search finds two files, not UTF16 needle; text_reads records NUL and replacement characters.
findings.causal_relevance: Known lossy intake behavior. No recorded failing source was established as non-UTF8 or oversized here.
findings.disposition: unresolved encoding/binary contract owned jointly with read callers; do not claim raw-byte fidelity

findings.finding: Whitespace decoding is not reversible; token slicing can corrupt multi-byte Unicode; cached tokenizer availability is not guaranteed offline on first use.
findings.causal_relevance: Known library limitations; default chunker stores raw text and does not decode token slices, so these facts alone do not explain its output.
findings.disposition: corrected false docstrings; no silent fallback or tokenizer redesign

findings.finding: Symbol metadata is approximate: missing Python parameter binding classes; wrong TS enum/type kind; type annotations counted as definitions; aliases overdefine imports.
findings.reproducible_evidence: intake_before.json#/symbols/decorated.py and sample.ts; intake_after.json#/symbols/sample.rs and sample.js.
findings.causal_relevance: Known local filtering/dependency errors. Resulting trace/selection effects on historical cases are hypotheses only.
findings.disposition: Python parameter sets and TS kinds fixed; semantic binding redesign not attempted

findings.finding: Symbol lane intentionally or structurally omits large definitions, decorator lines, malformed Python files and BOM-prefixed Python strings; tuple assignment bindings and Rust trait declarations are incomplete.
findings.reproducible_evidence: intake_after.json#/oversized_candidates is 0; symbols/invalid.py and bom.py are empty; decorated.py lacks decorator source; assignments.py and sample.rs show incomplete bindings.
findings.causal_relevance: Known symbol-lane loss, not proof of whole-pipeline absence: raw lexical chunks can still supply these sources.
findings.disposition: explicit limitations/recommendations; no speculative grammar/size policy expansion

findings.finding: Legacy Python window generator and tree-sitter-python dependency are not used by the production provider path.
findings.reproducible_evidence: Source grep of src and active eval/agent_bench/*.py plus eval/pasr_eval/**/*.py; Python provider imports ast; legacy generator only export/tests/new audit calls.
findings.causal_relevance: Not a demonstrated default-agent failure cause; dead-weight and public-API-maintenance concern.
findings.disposition: recommend removal only through explicit API/dependency cutover; preserve frozen study copies and current public exports

intake.test_coordination: AuditDiscovery owns its approved append to tests/test_tokenize.py; not counted as this slice's edit. New regression tests were added but no test suite/lint/formatter was run mid-flight; parent runs integration verification once. Actual smoke passed --verify.
intake.documentation: Updated owned module docstrings for cache freshness, discovery ignore scope, whitespace loss, offline tokenizer encoding data and candidate complete-line windows. Parent owns final changelog/docs integration.
limitations: No historical agent trace causal linkage assessed in this slice; all such relevance statements are hypotheses, not model/benchmark outcome claims.
File symlink creation unavailable on Windows without privilege (WinError 1314). Real directory junctions exercised root escapes; internal alias/cycle behavior remains unverified.
xd://lsp was requested and returned No such tool; parent notified. No public symbol/export removal was performed; source grep used for read-only reachability.

Baseline script initially hit a genuine leaked SQLite handle at tempfile cleanup. The retained baseline captures failed unlink, then forces garbage collection solely to permit cleanup. After correction unlink succeeds immediately.
Baseline NaN numeric observation is encoded as string NaN in intake_before.json to keep strict JSON validity; it represents an observed float NaN accepted by the old decoder.

Smoke script evolved to add origin recording, native Git NUL-delimited reference, junction checks, readonly writes, fresh offline encoding-cache failure, BOM and line-additive cases after baseline; those added scenarios have no before claim.
No statistical performance, memory, parser-version matrix, cold-model, paid API, cross-platform or full-suite evidence was generated here.

Global physical-line convention, hierarchical ignore behavior, binary/encoding policy, content-identity cache freshness and precise language binding graphs remain explicit design recommendations rather than partial silent migrations.

components.responsibility: Safe discovered-path ranking by token overlap; empty-query sorted listing.

reachability.default: Default MCP find_files and CLI find; callable library function. All candidates pass shared FileDiscoveryConfig restrictions before ranking.
reachability.optional: include and top_k; custom discovery config only on library API.
reachability.unwired: No semantic scorer, graph or persistent symbol/feature index.

components.rationale: Actual scoped literal stopword filename and listing operations succeed. Appropriate cheap navigation, not a substitute for content search.
risks: Bag-of-components ranking does not privilege exact full filename: gc.rs ties plugin_gc.rs and disable_gc.rs, while the rs extension also admits unrelated Rust files.
Prose containing a stopword filename can discard its useful component: where is where.py returns outside.py before scope/where.py on extension-only ties.
Shared allowed extensions, hidden/ignore settings and 200000-byte cap mean this is not a complete native filesystem glob.

components.responsibility: Definition lookup, literal usage scanning, content localization, bounded read guidance, and file-level lexical/similarity/reference ranking.

reachability.default: find_symbols/find_usages/find_evidence exposed by default MCP and CLI. Content search always computes lexical ranking, hashing similarity and lexical-seeded graph reranking for >=2 matching candidates. Symbol/content caches use EvidenceIndex.
reachability.optional: PASR_SEMANTIC_SCORER=minilm replaces hashing (not exercised; download prohibited); empty/none now disables similarity. Library default evidence top_k30/per_file2 differs from MCP top_k20/per_file1.
reachability.unwired: Graph weight/depth and path priors are internal constants, not user-facing MCP controls. find_usages bypasses persistent index and parses matching files through providers.

components.rationale: Fixed source-proven acronym false negatives and disabled-scorer crash, corrected causal/graph comments, removed unused _RRF_K and duplicate depth comment. Retain default ranking until answer-level ablation can resolve mixed evidence.

subcomponents.name: definition lookup
subcomponents.value: Exact PluginGc returns struct before impl; case-exact Where ranks class before where function; alias class works, unsupported .go is surfaced and wrong-kind filtering lists available kinds.

subcomponents.name: literal usage scan
subcomponents.value: Cross-file real PluginGc definitions/usages include line text and owners; whole-word query and top_k truncation work. Keep description literal; no semantic binding guarantee.

subcomponents.name: lexical content gate and IDF
subcomponents.value: Cheap topical gate finds real snippets; corrected acronym splitting aligns with existing identifier_terms. Substring document counts intentionally differ from whole-word hit eligibility.

subcomponents.name: hashing similarity
subcomponents.value: Nushell gc/signals target ranks improve 3->1; recursion eval_ir 67->26; rust-analyzer reload worsens12->14. Demonstrated retrieval-rank changes, not model understanding or answer accuracy. Cannot bridge arbitrary synonyms or expand candidates.

subcomponents.name: reference graph reranking
subcomponents.value: Mixed: PASR index9->2 and Nushell gc3->1, but rust-analyzer reload12->73 and Nushell eval_ir67->118. References include comments/string names, plus uniform dangling redistribution; no semantic resolution.

subcomponents.name: length normalization and fixture/prose priors
subcomponents.value: Active heuristics; existing regression fixtures and historical claims exist, but this audit does not independently isolate answer-level value. A fixture or document can itself be the requested answer, so source comments claiming they cannot contain answers are not universal.

subcomponents.name: persistent parsed definitions/block features
subcomponents.value: Cache disabled/cold/warm fixture outputs identical. AuditIntake owns corruption/precision fixes. Timings here confound disk and process parse caches and do not isolate index speed.

subcomponents.name: read_lines and compact hit text
subcomponents.value: Actual 40-line functions receive complete range; 41-line function receives +/-8 neighborhood; only first5 hits get guidance. Treat as navigation suggestions, not guaranteed evidence coverage.

subcomponents.name: _RRF_K
subcomponents.value: Unused constant removed; evidence search uses additive scaled rank, not reciprocal-rank fusion.

risks: Candidate gate is lexical substring inclusion; graph and similarity cannot recover a zero-overlap target. Only first250 lexical candidates receive additional scores.
Every evidence call reads every discovered file; all substring-matching files get definitions, even if later they yield no hits. top_k limits output, not this work.
First160 stripped characters can omit the matching term; per_file truncation and top_k constrain delivered lines, and read_lines is absent after first5.
Empty find_symbols query indexes files but returns no matches; unsupported languages are reported, parse failures can still return no definitions.
Scorer environment is captured at import and scorer cached; invalid names/missing optional package silently fall back to hashing.

findings.title: Graph reranking can remove a relevant lexical candidate from the delivered window
findings.observed: rust-analyzer query background indexing idle busy state: reload.rs lexical12, similarity14, graph73, blend78. Nushell recursion count limit: eval_ir.rs lexical67, similarity26, graph118, blend50. MCP default20 cannot include those blended targets.

causal_relevance.explanation: This proves a current retrieval mechanism can lose access within an output cap, not that these self-chosen queries caused any recorded model failure. Historical run attribution belongs to trace audit; no model was run.

findings.disposition: unresolved: keep default pending targeted answer-level ablation; do not infer global removal from five rank probes. Counterexamples included.

findings.title: Semantic and graph names overstate actual candidate reach
findings.observed: api.py mentions idle/stop and references Collector; engine.py defines Collector but contains neither query term. find_evidence(idle stop) returns only api.py. Graph nodes are the lexical top250; a query-term-free target is never a candidate.

causal_relevance.explanation: Native grep/reads can follow a newly learned identifier to engine.py in a subsequent call. PASR find_symbols/find_usages can too if the agent chooses that move; graph itself does not eliminate the hop.

findings.disposition: change explanatory claims, retain behavior; broader semantic expansion is a redesign, not a small audit fix.

findings.title: Acronym-prefixed identifiers had positive file counts but no returned matching line

causal_relevance.explanation: Consumer-visible false negative proved, but no supplied frozen run is attributed to it.

findings.disposition: fixed: reuse existing identifier_terms for acronym-aware line terms; behavioral regression added.

findings.title: Disabled semantic scorer crashed searches with multiple candidates
findings.before: PASR_SEMANTIC_SCORER none or empty returned None from factory, then AttributeError: NoneType object has no attribute score.
findings.after: Returns matching lines using lexical + graph rank, with no similarity contribution.

causal_relevance.explanation: Default hashing is unaffected; no evidence that recorded agents used disabled scorer configuration.

findings.disposition: fixed; empty and none regression cases return rare evidence.

findings.title: Documented tokenizer protocol failed in legacy candidate generators
findings.before: MinimalTokenizer.encode(text) rejected unexpected truncation keyword in fallback.
findings.after: Bare-text encoder produces real lexical candidate token span; nested batch works; unrelated internal TypeError is propagated.

causal_relevance.explanation: Legacy/direct-library utility, not the current default RawSpan selector path.

findings.disposition: fixed documented protocol without changing public API.

findings.title: Qualified usage fallback is lexical, conditional, and can be blocked by a comment
findings.observed: Signals::check returns only a documentation comment, no bare fallback; Other::check with zero qualified hits retries check and returns unrelated Python/Rust names. Real Signals::interrupted retries interrupted and returns nu-glob definitions before the Signals method, 4 definitions and54 usage lines overall.

causal_relevance.explanation: May consume follow-up budget or suggest the wrong owner; no specific frozen error assigned without delivered-history analysis.

findings.disposition: keep literal contract and searched field; clarify it is not semantic reference resolution. Do not silently broaden matching on any qualified result.

findings.title: A localization hit is not the full evidence and its count is not raw occurrence count
findings.observed: checkpoint at end of long line is not present in delivered160-character text; eight matching functions produce hit_count2 under per_file2; usage8 gets read_lines on first5 only. 40-line function read1-40, 41-line function read53-69 around hit61. Larger body must be explicitly selected/read.

causal_relevance.explanation: A locator or source filename in history cannot be counted as delivered mechanism evidence. Missing surrounding lines may be selection/agent follow-up, not never locating a file.

findings.disposition: keep compact navigation contract; do not use these counts/hints as proof of evidence completeness.

findings.title: Substring document counts and whole-identifier line eligibility describe different populations
findings.observed: point query on checkpoint yields files_with_a_match1, term_file_counts.point1, hit_count0. Positive counts are not evidence of a returnable line, and these silent candidates still participate in file ranking work.

causal_relevance.explanation: Could confuse follow-up and IDF calibration; no recorded answer outcome attributed.

findings.disposition: document distinction, no unmeasured global boundary-ranking retune.

findings.title: Explicit missing include is not equivalent across direct library and MCP surface
findings.observed: Direct nonexistent include returns files_scanned0 with no hits; empty include list means whole workspace; ../ raises ValueError. MCP wraps include through _usable_include, so this direct-call observation is not a claim about delivered MCP scope warnings.

causal_relevance.explanation: Integration audit owns MCP widening/advice; library evidence alone cannot attribute scope failures.

findings.disposition: keep current library contracts and audit transport separately.

reachability_evidence: src/pasr/symbols/__init__.py:legacy generator retained for direct callers

mechanism_value_summary.demonstrated: Exact path/symbol/usage navigation works on real Nushell checkout; hashing and graph can improve some target ranks and degrade others; corrected acronym search has an actual before/after false-negative repair.
mechanism_value_summary.not_demonstrated: No answer accuracy, native-vs-PASR win, general semantic understanding, globally optimal weights/depth/priors, or isolated component speedup follows from these probes.
mechanism_value_summary.expense: Content top_k/per_file cap output only; every discovered file is read, every substring-match candidate has definitions loaded/computed, only250 receive similarity and graph. Ablation weights zero out contributions but still execute scorers, so ablation timing is NOT a lexical-vs-graph CPU comparison.

test_review_notes: Existing tests/test_symbol_search.py:test_a_path_that_cannot_hold_an_implementation_is_ranked_below_one_that_can directly checks path-prior constants; it is not evidence of end-to-end fixture demotion or benchmark value. Parent owns incidental-test cleanup; not re-pinned here.
limitations: No paid APIs, local LLMs, embeddings, downloads, benchmark answering or frozen artifact edits. All smoke paths are real production functions; weight/cache patching only disables contributions/storage, not returned data.

Real checkout probes copied already-discovered crates/src (Nushell), crates/lib (rust-analyzer), and src (PASR) into temporary workspaces to avoid changing real checkout caches. These are explicit scope probes, not the frozen agent-study root/snapshot.

Queries are audit-selected mechanism probes, not all recorded model queries. Target ranks are deterministic retrieval diagnostics only. Do not compare these to frozen outcomes or infer answer causality.

Intermediate discovery_after predates acronym fix; discovery_final includes it. Current comments/dead-constant cleanup was made during the final checkout run and does not change executed behavior; discovery_smoke_verified records latest owned source hashes/origins and assertions.

Source dependencies were concurrently audited. Final PASR-self ranking moved from lexical7 to9 as its source changed; final artifact is authoritative for its measured snapshot, not evidence of a rank regression.

Cache cold/warm/disabled equality is exercised on a small fixture only. Repeated process-level parse/features and OS caches confound raw elapsed times; no isolated cache speedup claim. Persistent index schema/corruption/precision testing belongs to AuditIntake.
Minilm and actual Hugging Face/tensor implementations not loaded; dependency-free shape-compatible adapter exercised. Empty/none scorer configuration was executed directly.
LSP device unavailable in child; parent queried encode_ids/decode_ids and got declarations only. Explicit grep confirmed legacy callers; no public exports removed.

scenarios.after: ValueError from name validation before writing the file.

observations.quote:
[src/click/termui.py:91-187]
    """Prompts a user for input.  This is a convenience function that can
    be used to prompt a user for input later.

    If the user aborts the input by sending an interrupt signal, this
    function will catch it and raise a :exc:`Abort` exception.

    :param text: the text to show for the prompt.
    :param default: the default value to use if no input happens.  If this
                    is not given it will prompt until it's aborted.
    :param hide_input: if this is set to true then the input value will
                       be hidden.
    :param confirmation_prompt: Prompt a second time to confirm the
        value. Can be set to a string instead of ``True`` to customize
        the message.
    :param type: the type to use to check the value against.
    :param value_proc: if this parameter is provided it's a function that
                       is invoked instead of the type conversion to
                       convert a value.
    :param prompt_suffix: a suffix that should be added to the prompt.
    :param show_default: shows or hides the default value in the prompt.
    :param err: if set to true the file defaults to ``stderr`` instead of
                ``stdout``, the same as with echo.
    :param show_choices: Show or hide choices if the passed type is a Choice.
                         For example if type is a Choice of either day or week,
                         show_choices is true and text is "Group by" then the
                         prompt will be "Group by (day, week): ".

    .. versionadded:: 8.0
        ``confirmation_prompt`` can be a custom string.

    .. versionadded:: 7.0
        Added the ``show_choices`` parameter.

    .. versionadded:: 6.0
        Added unicode support for cmd.exe on Windows.

    .. versionadded:: 4.0
        Added the `err` parameter.

    """

    def prompt_func(text: str) -> str:
        f = hidden_prompt_func if hide_input else visible_prompt_func
        try:
            # Write the prompt separately so that we get nice
            # coloring through colorama on Windows
            echo(text.rstrip(" "), nl=False, err=err)
            # Echo a space to stdout to work around an issue where
            # readline causes backspace to clear the whole line.
            return f(" ")
        except (KeyboardInterrupt, EOFError):
            # getpass doesn't print a newline if the user aborts input with ^C.
            # Allegedly this behavior is inherited from getpass(3).
            # A doc bug has been filed at https://bugs.python.org/issue24711
            if hide_input:
                echo(None, err=err)
            raise Abort() from None

    if value_proc is None:
        value_proc = convert_type(type, default)

    prompt = _build_prompt(
        text, prompt_suffix, show_default, default, show_choices, type
    )

    if confirmation_prompt:
        if confirmation_prompt is True:
            confirmation_prompt = _("Repeat for confirmation")

        confirmation_prompt = _build_prompt(confirmation_prompt, prompt_suffix)

    while True:
        while True:
            value = prompt_func(prompt)
            if value:
                break
            elif default is not None:
                value = default
                break
        try:
            result = value_proc(value)
        except UsageError as e:
            if hide_input:
                echo(_("Error: The value you entered was invalid."), err=err)
            else:

def default_if_none(default=NOTHING, factory=None):
    """
    A converter that allows to replace `None` values by *default* or the result
    of *factory*.

    Args:
        default:
            Value to be used if `None` is passed. Passing an instance of
            `attrs.Factory` is supported, however the ``takes_self`` option is
            *not*.

        factory (typing.Callable):
            A callable that takes no parameters whose result is used if `None`
            is passed.

    Raises:
        TypeError: If **neither** *default* or *factory* is passed.

        TypeError: If **both** *default* and *factory* are passed.

        ValueError:
            If an instance of `attrs.Factory` is passed with
            ``takes_self=True``.

    .. versionadded:: 18.2.0
    """
    if default is NOTHING and factory is None:
        msg = "Must pass either `default` or `factory`."
        raise TypeError(msg)

    if default is not NOTHING and factory is not None:
        msg = "Must pass either `default` or `factory` but not both."
        raise TypeError(msg)

    if factory is not None:
        default = Factory(factory)

    if isinstance(default, Factory):
        if default.takes_self:
            msg = "`takes_self` is not supported by default_if_none."
            raise ValueError(msg)

        def default_if_none_converter(val):
            if val is not None:
                return val

            return default.factory()

    else:

        def default_if_none_converter(val):
            if val is not None:
                return val

            return default

    return default_if_none_converter

    def merge_environment_settings(self, url, proxies, stream, verify, cert):
        """
        Check the environment and merge it with some settings.

        :rtype: dict
        """

def merge_setting(request_setting, session_setting, dict_class=OrderedDict):
    """Determines appropriate setting for a given request, taking into account
    the explicit setting on that request, and the setting in the session. If a
    setting is a dictionary, they will be merged together using `dict_class`
    """

    if session_setting is None:
        return request_setting

    if request_setting is None:
        return session_setting

    # Bypass if not a dictionary (e.g. verify)
    if not (
        isinstance(session_setting, Mapping) and isinstance(request_setting, Mapping)
    ):
        return request_setting

    merged_setting = dict_class(to_key_val_list(session_setting))
    merged_setting.update(to_key_val_list(request_setting))

    # Remove keys that are set to None. Extract keys first to avoid altering
    # the dictionary during iteration.
    none_keys = [k for (k, v) in merged_setting.items() if v is None]
    for key in none_keys:
        del merged_setting[key]

    return merged_setting

def merge_setting(request_setting, session_setting, dict_class=OrderedDict):
    """Determines appropriate setting for a given request, taking into account
    the explicit setting on that request, and the setting in the session. If a
    setting is a dictionary, they will be merged together using `dict_class`
    """

    if session_setting is None:
        return request_setting

    if request_setting is None:
        return session_setting

    # Bypass if not a dictionary (e.g. verify)
    if not (
        isinstance(session_setting, Mapping) and isinstance(request_setting, Mapping)
    ):
        return request_setting

    merged_setting = dict_class(to_key_val_list(session_setting))
    merged_setting.update(to_key_val_list(request_setting))

    # Remove keys that are set to None. Extract keys first to avoid altering
    # the dictionary during iteration.
    none_keys = [k for (k, v) in merged_setting.items() if v is None]
    for key in none_keys:
        del merged_setting[key]

    return merged_setting

rows.question: A cookie jar contains cookies with the same name on different domains or paths. How do bracket lookup and get differ when looking up that name, how can the collision be narrowed, and what does this checkout do for a single matching cookie whose value is the empty string?
rows.answer:
Bracket lookup (`jar[name]`) and `jar.get(name)` both use the same lookup logic: they return a value only if exactly one cookie matches, and raise `CookieConflictError` if multiple cookies with that name match. To narrow the match, pass `domain=` and/or `path=` to `get`, for example `jar.get(name, domain="example.com", path="/")`; the error class also recommends those arguments ( `src/requests/cookies.py:170-173, 387-431`).

There’s an empty-string edge case in this checkout: the lookup tracks a match by storing its value, then returns only if that value is truthy. So a single matching cookie whose value is `""` results in `KeyError`, not `""` (`src/requests/cookies.py:387-431`).

rows.question: How does dependency-group lookup differ from full resolution when groups include other groups? Explain name normalization, expansion order, caching, and how cyclic includes affect repeated resolution attempts.
rows.answer:
`lookup()` and `resolve()` both normalize the requested group name, but they do different work: `lookup()` returns parsed entries as-is and **does not follow includes**, while `resolve()` expands included groups into requirements (`src/packaging/dependency_groups.py:134-167`). Group names are normalized when the resolver ingests the mapping, and include names are normalized again before resolution (`src/packaging/dependency_groups.py:124-127, 180-181`).

Full resolution walks each group’s entries in order: it appends direct requirements where they appear and recursively appends an included group’s resolved requirements at that include’s position (`src/packaging/dependency_groups.py:183-205`). Parsed groups are cached separately from completed resolutions, so parsing work is reused; successful resolutions are cached by normalized group name (`src/packaging/dependency_groups.py:124-127, 222`). Cycle detection tracks each group’s ancestors while traversing includes; `lookup()` can therefore return an include that would be cyclic without raising a cycle error, whereas `resolve()` reports the cycle (`src/packaging/dependency_groups.py:134-167`; `tests/test_dependency_groups.py:96-106`).

If resolution encounters errors, it returns an empty result for that group **without caching it**. The code explicitly says this lets repeated attempts to resolve a cyclic group raise errors again rather than reusing a cached result (`src/packaging/dependency_groups.py:211-219`).

criteria.description: lookup normalizes the requested name and parses the group without resolving includes; resolve normalizes then invokes recursive resolution under an error collector. Normalization lowercases names and replaces each run of hyphens, underscores, or dots with one hyphen, so names differing only in case or those separator runs are equivalent.
criteria.frozen_answer_quote: Group names are normalized when the resolver ingests the mapping, and include names are normalized again before resolution

def lookup(self, group: str) -> tuple[Requirement | DependencyGroupInclude, ...]:
        """
        Lookup a group name, returning the parsed dependency data for that group.
        This will not resolve includes.

        :param group: the name of the group to lookup
        """
        group = _normalize_name(group)

        with _ErrorCollector().on_exit(
            f"[dependency-groups] data for {group!r} was malformed"
        ) as errors:
            return self._parse_group(group, errors)

    def resolve(self, group: str) -> tuple[Requirement, ...]:
        """
        Resolve a dependency group to a list of requirements.

        :param group: the name of the group to resolve
        """
        group = _normalize_name(group)

        with _ErrorCollector().on_exit(
            f"[dependency-groups] data for {group!r} was malformed"

rows.question: How does a session combine caller-supplied proxies and TLS verification settings with environment variables and session defaults? Explain when environment values are ignored, how an explicit proxy entry wins, and what a proxy value of None does during merging.
rows.answer:
With `trust_env` enabled, `merge_environment_settings` first adds environment proxies using `proxies.setdefault`, then consults `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE` or `CURL_CA_BUNDLE` only when the request’s `verify` value is `True` or `None` (`src/requests/sessions.py:750–779`). So environment proxy values fill only missing keys; an explicit proxy entry for a key already in the caller’s `proxies` dict wins. When `trust_env` is disabled, that environment-processing block is skipped.

Afterward, request settings are merged with session defaults. For dictionaries such as proxies, the session mapping is copied first and the request mapping updates it, so caller entries take precedence (`src/requests/sessions.py:61–88`). Any proxy key whose merged value is `None` is then removed—`None` does not mean “use the session or environment proxy”; it suppresses that key. For non-dictionary settings such as `verify`, a non-`None` request value takes precedence over the session value, while `None` falls back to the session setting; the session’s default `verify` is `True` (`src/requests/sessions.py:61–88, 417–425`).

rows.question: When iter_content is called on a response, how does it choose between an unread raw stream and previously cached content, and how are stream failures and optional Unicode decoding handled? Include what happens if the stream was consumed without a reusable body.
rows.answer:
`iter_content` creates both a raw-stream generator and an iterator that slices `self._content`, then selects between them based on `self._content_consumed`: an unconsumed response reads from the raw stream; a consumed response replays cached content in chunks (`src/requests/models.py:816–855`). If the response is marked consumed but `_content` is still a boolean rather than reusable body data, it raises `StreamConsumedError` instead of trying to replay it (`src/requests/models.py:839–840`).

For urllib3-style raw objects, it calls `self.raw.stream(chunk_size, decode_content=True)` and translates `ProtocolError`, `DecodeError`, `ReadTimeoutError`, and `SSLError` into Requests’ `ChunkedEncodingError`, `ContentDecodingError`, `ConnectionError`, and `RequestsSSLError`, respectively (`src/requests/models.py:818–828`). For other raw objects, it repeatedly calls `read(chunk_size)` and stops on an empty result (`src/requests/models.py:829–835`). The generator marks content consumed after reading completes (`src/requests/models.py:837`).

With `decode_unicode=True`, the chosen chunks are passed through `stream_decode_response_unicode`. If the response has no encoding, that helper yields the original chunks; otherwise, it uses an incremental decoder with replacement for decoding errors and emits any final buffered text (`src/requests/models.py:852–854`; `src/requests/utils.py:564–578`).

rows.question: How does click.prompt handle empty input, conversion failures, and confirmation mismatches without exposing invalid hidden input? Explain whether confirmation compares converted values or the original inputs, and what happens on EOF or Ctrl-C.
rows.answer:
`click.prompt` treats an empty first response as “use the default” when a default exists; without one, it prompts again. It converts the resulting value before returning it. If conversion raises `UsageError`, it retries: visible prompts show the error message, while hidden prompts show only “The value you entered was invalid,” so the invalid hidden input is not disclosed (`src/click/termui.py`, `prompt`, lines 146–163).

With confirmation enabled, an empty confirmation is accepted when both responses are empty; otherwise it keeps prompting until the confirmation is nonempty. It compares the **original input strings** (`value == value2`), not converted results, and reports a mismatch generically. For hidden input, neither the mismatch nor conversion error reveals the entered value (`src/click/termui.py`, `prompt`, lines 164–187).

EOF and Ctrl-C (KeyboardInterrupt) are caught by the prompt helper and raised as `click.Abort`; for hidden input it first emits a newline (`src/click/termui.py`, `prompt_func`, lines 124–135).

material_clauses.answer_evidence:
`click.prompt` treats an empty first response as “use the default” when a default exists; without one, it prompts again. It converts the resulting value before returning it. If conversion raises `UsageError`, it retries: visible prompts show the error message, while hidden prompts show only “The value you entered was invalid,” so the invalid hidden input is not disclosed (`src/click/termui.py`, `prompt`, lines 146–163).

With confirmation enabled, an empty confirmation is accepted when both responses are empty; otherwise it keeps prompting until the confirmation is nonempty. It compares the **original input strings** (`value == value2`), not converted results, and reports a mismatch generically. For hidden input, neither the mismatch nor conversion error reveals the entered value (`src/click/termui.py`, `prompt`, lines 164–187).

EOF and Ctrl-C (KeyboardInterrupt) are caught by the prompt helper and raised as `click.Abort`; for hidden input it first emits a newline (`src/click/termui.py`, `prompt_func`, lines 124–135).

rows.question: Compare not_ and or_ when child validators succeed or raise. Which exceptions count as an inverted success, when does an OR stop, and how does nested OR composition affect execution?
rows.answer:
`not_` treats a child exception as an inverted success only when it matches `exc_types`, which defaults to `(ValueError, TypeError)`; it suppresses that exception. If the child returns normally, `not_` raises `ValueError`. Exceptions outside the configured types are not intercepted and pass through (`src/attr/validators.py`, `not_` and `_NotValidator.__call__`).

`_OrValidator.__call__` tries children in order: any child that returns normally makes the OR succeed immediately, while any raised `Exception` is caught and the next child is tried. If every child raises, the OR raises `ValueError` (`src/attr/validators.py`, `_OrValidator.__call__`). I could not determine how the `or_` factory handles nested ORs—specifically whether it flattens them or leaves them nested—so I can’t establish how that affects execution.

rows.question: How does default_if_none choose between a fixed replacement and a factory when an attribute receives None? Explain what happens for non-None input and which invalid configurations fail before conversion.
rows.answer:
`default_if_none` accepts either a fixed `default` or a zero-argument `factory`. If `factory` is supplied, it wraps it in an `attrs.Factory`; if `default` itself is an `attrs.Factory`, that is also treated as a factory. When the input is `None`, the converter calls the factory and returns its result, or returns the fixed default; when the input is non-`None`, it returns that input unchanged (`src/attr/converters.py:89–109`).

The configuration is checked when `default_if_none(...)` is called, before any value is converted: passing neither option or passing both raises `TypeError`, and an `attrs.Factory` with `takes_self=True` raises `ValueError` (`src/attr/converters.py:81–95`).

rows.question: When a Typer application raises a developer exception, how does it arrange custom traceback display, and when does it fall back to the original exception hook? Explain the Rich and non-Rich paths and what short tracebacks do to internal frames.
rows.answer:
`Typer.__call__` in `typer/main.py` installs `except_hook` as `sys.excepthook` if it is not already installed, then tags exceptions raised while invoking the command with the app’s pretty-exception settings before re-raising them.

The hook delegates to the original exception hook when `TYPER_STANDARD_TRACEBACK` (or its fallback `_TYPER_STANDARD_TRACEBACK`) is set, when the exception lacks Typer’s developer-exception tag, or when pretty exceptions are disabled. Otherwise, it identifies Typer and Click’s internal directories. With Rich available, it calls `rich_utils.get_traceback(...)` and prints the result to stderr; without Rich, it builds and prints a standard `TracebackException` after filtering its frames.

In the non-Rich path, short tracebacks omit Typer and Click frames entirely. When short tracebacks are disabled, those internal frames remain, but their source-code lines are blanked. I can’t determine the Rich renderer’s precise handling of internal frames or short tracebacks from the source details available here.

rows.question: How does click.prompt handle empty input, conversion failures, and confirmation mismatches without exposing invalid hidden input? Explain whether confirmation compares converted values or the original inputs, and what happens on EOF or Ctrl-C.
rows.answer:
`click.prompt` reads through `prompt_func`, which selects `hidden_prompt_func` (`getpass`) when `hide_input=True`; it catches both `KeyboardInterrupt` (Ctrl-C) and `EOFError` there and raises `click.Abort`. For hidden input, it also emits a newline before aborting because `getpass` may not do so (src/click/termui.py:132–147).

An empty first response is retried when there is no default; with a default, the default is used instead (lines 162–169). The value is then converted by `value_proc` (or the type converter); a `UsageError` causes another attempt. Hidden prompts show only a generic invalid-value message, not the entered value or the conversion error detail (lines 170–177).

With confirmation enabled, Click prompts again and compares the **original input strings**, not the converted results: it returns the already-converted result only when `value == value2` (lines 178–187). An empty confirmation is retried unless both the original value and confirmation are empty; that special case allows an empty/default input to confirm (lines 180–184). A mismatch prints a generic mismatch message and restarts the outer prompt loop; hidden input itself is not echoed by this logic.

rows.question: A cookie jar contains cookies with the same name on different domains or paths. How do bracket lookup and get differ when looking up that name, how can the collision be narrowed, and what does this checkout do for a single matching cookie whose value is the empty string?
rows.answer:
Bracket lookup, `jar[name]`, requires an unambiguous match: it raises `CookieConflictError` if more than one cookie matches the name. `jar.get(name, default=None, domain=None, path=None)` uses the same matching logic, but lets you pass `domain` and/or `path` to narrow the search; if no match is found, it returns the default (`src/requests/cookies.py:194–204, 327–334, 386–407`).

For a single matching cookie whose value is `""`, this checkout treats it as missing: the lookup helper checks `if toReturn:` and raises `KeyError` for the empty value (`src/requests/cookies.py:409–413`). Consequently, bracket lookup raises `KeyError`, while `get` returns its default.

rows.question: How does dependency-group lookup differ from full resolution when groups include other groups? Explain name normalization, expansion order, caching, and how cyclic includes affect repeated resolution attempts.
rows.answer:
`lookup()` and `resolve()` both normalize the requested group name by replacing runs of `-`, `_`, or `.` with `-` and lowercasing it; group names in the table are normalized the same way, and collisions are rejected as duplicate names (`src/packaging/dependency_groups.py:120`, `:133–145`, `:153–158`, `:307–335`). The key difference is that `lookup()` parses only that group and returns include markers as `DependencyGroupInclude` objects—it does not follow them—whereas `resolve()` recursively expands each include in place, preserving the order of ordinary requirements and included requirements (`:133–145`, `:147–158`, `:177–203`). Include names are normalized before following them, too (`:182–184`).

The resolver caches parsed groups separately from successful resolutions: `_parsed_groups` avoids parsing a group again, while `_resolve_cache` stores completed requirement tuples (`:122–129`, `:218–223`, `:274–278`, `:172–175`, `:215–216`). During expansion it tracks ancestors to detect a path that loops back to a group (`:185–203`). If resolution encounters errors—including a cycle—it returns an empty result for that group and does not cache it, so a later resolution attempt can traverse it again and report the cycle again (`:209–215`). Tests confirm lookup alone does not trigger a cycle, while resolving a cyclic include raises `CyclicDependencyGroup` (`tests/test_dependency_groups.py:96–107`, `:263–285`).

criteria.description: lookup normalizes the requested name and parses the group without resolving includes; resolve normalizes then invokes recursive resolution under an error collector. Normalization lowercases names and replaces each run of hyphens, underscores, or dots with one hyphen, so names differing only in case or those separator runs are equivalent.
criteria.frozen_answer_quote: replacing runs of `-`, `_`, or `.` with `-` and lowercasing it

def lookup(self, group: str) -> tuple[Requirement | DependencyGroupInclude, ...]:
        """
        Lookup a group name, returning the parsed dependency data for that group.
        This will not resolve includes.

        :param group: the name of the group to lookup
        """
        group = _normalize_name(group)

        with _ErrorCollector().on_exit(
            f"[dependency-groups] data for {group!r} was malformed"
        ) as errors:
            return self._parse_group(group, errors)

    def resolve(self, group: str) -> tuple[Requirement, ...]:
        """
        Resolve a dependency group to a list of requirements.

        :param group: the name of the group to resolve
        """
        group = _normalize_name(group)

        with _ErrorCollector().on_exit(
            f"[dependency-groups] data for {group!r} was malformed"
        ) as errors:
            return self._resolve(group, group, errors)

rows.question: When iter_content is called on a response, how does it choose between an unread raw stream and previously cached content, and how are stream failures and optional Unicode decoding handled? Include what happens if the stream was consumed without a reusable body.
rows.answer:
`iter_content` reads from the underlying `raw` stream when content has not yet been consumed; if `_content_consumed` is already true, it replays chunks from the cached `_content` instead. If the stream was consumed without a reusable cached body (`_content is False`), it raises `StreamConsumedError` rather than trying to read the stream again. [src/requests/models.py:799–814]

For urllib3 streams, it delegates to `raw.stream(chunk_size, decode_content=True)` and translates failures: `ProtocolError` to `ChunkedEncodingError`, `DecodeError` to `ContentDecodingError`, `ReadTimeoutError` to `ConnectionError`, and `SSLError` to `RequestsSSLError`. For a standard file-like `raw`, it repeatedly calls `read(chunk_size)` until it gets no data. [src/requests/models.py:816–837]

With `decode_unicode=True`, it passes the generated chunks through `stream_decode_response_unicode`, which decodes using the response encoding when one is available; otherwise, the chunks remain as-is. [src/requests/models.py:838–839]

criteria.description: The raw stream path calls raw.stream(chunk_size, decode_content=True); a standard file-like object is read until an empty chunk.
criteria.frozen_answer_quote: For urllib3 streams, it delegates to `raw.stream(chunk_size, decode_content=True)`

rows.question: How does dependency-group lookup differ from full resolution when groups include other groups? Explain name normalization, expansion order, caching, and how cyclic includes affect repeated resolution attempts.
rows.answer:
`lookup()` normalizes the requested name and parses that group, but deliberately **does not expand includes**; its result can contain `DependencyGroupInclude` objects. `resolve()` also normalizes the requested name, then recursively expands includes into requirements (`src/packaging/dependency_groups.py:136–167`).

Group names are normalized by replacing runs matched by `_NORMALIZE_PATTERN` with `-` and lowercasing. Included names are normalized too, when resolution encounters them (`src/packaging/dependency_groups.py:186–188, 310–311`).

Expansion follows the group’s parsed item order: requirements are appended where they occur, and each include is recursively resolved and spliced in at that position (`src/packaging/dependency_groups.py:174–198`). The resolver caches parsed groups and completed resolutions separately; a successful resolution is cached by normalized group name (`src/packaging/dependency_groups.py:124–130, 169–170, 215–216`). If errors have been found, it returns an empty tuple for that group and does **not** cache the result. In particular, cyclic includes therefore remain uncached, so repeated resolution attempts can report the cycle again (`src/packaging/dependency_groups.py:204–213`).

Normalization lowercases names and replaces each run of hyphens, underscores, or dots with one hyphen, so names differing only in case or those separator runs are equivalent.

def lookup(self, group: str) -> tuple[Requirement | DependencyGroupInclude, ...]:
        """
        Lookup a group name, returning the parsed dependency data for that group.
        This will not resolve includes.

        :param group: the name of the group to lookup
        """
        group = _normalize_name(group)

        with _ErrorCollector().on_exit(
            f"[dependency-groups] data for {group!r} was malformed"
        ) as errors:
            return self._parse_group(group, errors)

    def resolve(self, group: str) -> tuple[Requirement, ...]:
        """
        Resolve a dependency group to a list of requirements.

        :param group: the name of the group to resolve
        """
        group = _normalize_name(group)

        with _ErrorCollector().on_exit(
            f"[dependency-groups] data for {group!r} was malformed"
        ) as errors:
            return self._resolve(group, group, errors)

rows.question: Compare not_ and or_ when child validators succeed or raise. Which exceptions count as an inverted success, when does an OR stop, and how does nested OR composition affect execution?
rows.answer:
`not_` treats a child validator as an **inverted success** only when it raises one of the configured `exc_types` (default `(ValueError, TypeError)`); those exceptions are suppressed (src/attr/validators.py:611–615, 632–637). If the child returns normally, `not_` raises `ValueError`; exceptions outside `exc_types` pass through unchanged (lines 617–626, 649–651).

`or_` tries children in order and stops at the first one that returns normally. Any `Exception` raised by a child counts as failure for that branch, so it continues; if every child raises, `or_` raises its own `ValueError` (lines 672–682).

Nested ORs are flattened when `or_` is constructed: a child `_OrValidator` contributes its validators directly to the parent’s sequence (lines 707–711). Consequently, nested OR composition executes as one ordered list, stopping at the first successful child rather than treating the inner OR as a separate execution boundary.

rows.question: What happens when an already-registered plugin name is blocked and later unblocked? Trace removal of its hook implementations, the blocked-name representation, and whether unblocking restores the original plugin.
rows.answer: When `set_blocked(name)` is called, it first calls `unregister(name=name)` and then stores `None` for that name in `_name2plugin` (`src/pluggy/_manager.py`, `set_blocked`). `unregister` removes the plugin’s implementations from each hook caller via `hookcaller._remove_plugin(plugin)`; because the name is blocked, it leaves the `None` entry in the name map rather than deleting it (`src/pluggy/_manager.py`, `unregister`). That `None` value is the blocked-name representation: `unblock(name)` detects it, deletes the entry, and returns `True` (`src/pluggy/_manager.py`, `unblock`). Unblocking only clears the block; it does **not** restore the original plugin or its hook implementations. The test confirms the name can be registered again after unblocking, but with a newly supplied plugin (`testing/test_pluginmanager.py`, `test_set_blocked`). I could not determine from the returned code whether the original plugin object is retained elsewhere; the shown manager operations do not restore it.

def set_blocked(self, name: str) -> None:
        """Block registrations of the given name, unregister if already registered."""
        self.unregister(name=name)
        self._name2plugin[name] = None

    def is_blocked(self, name: str) -> bool:
        """Return whether the given plugin name is blocked."""
        return name in self._name2plugin and self._name2plugin[name] is None

rows.question: When iter_content is called on a response, how does it choose between an unread raw stream and previously cached content, and how are stream failures and optional Unicode decoding handled? Include what happens if the stream was consumed without a reusable body.
rows.answer: In `Response.iter_content`, Requests reads from `self.raw` when the response body has not yet been consumed; it uses `self.raw.stream(..., decode_content=True)` when available, or repeatedly calls `self.raw.read()` for a standard file-like object (`src/requests/models.py:816-837`). After consumption, it re-slices the cached `_content` into chunks instead (`src/requests/models.py:845-850`). If `_content` is still a boolean at that point—meaning the stream was consumed without a reusable cached body—it raises `StreamConsumedError` rather than trying to read the raw stream again (`src/requests/models.py:839-840`). The urllib3 stream path translates protocol, content-decoding, read-timeout, and SSL errors respectively into `ChunkedEncodingError`, `ContentDecodingError`, `ConnectionError`, and Requests’ `SSLError` (`src/requests/models.py:818-828`). If `decode_unicode=True`, it wraps the chosen chunk iterator in `stream_decode_response_unicode`; otherwise chunks are returned without that decoding step (`src/requests/models.py:852-854`).

rows.question: When a Typer application raises a developer exception, how does it arrange custom traceback display, and when does it fall back to the original exception hook? Explain the Rich and non-Rich paths and what short tracebacks do to internal frames.
rows.answer:
Typer’s `except_hook` in `typer/main.py` saves the original `sys.excepthook`, then looks for Typer’s developer-exception configuration on the exception itself. It delegates to the original hook if `TYPER_STANDARD_TRACEBACK` (or its underscored fallback) is set, the exception has no Typer configuration, or pretty exceptions are disabled (`typer/main.py`, `except_hook`, lines 57–75).

Otherwise, Typer identifies its and Click’s package directories as internal paths. With Rich available, it builds a traceback via `rich_utils.get_traceback` and prints it to stderr. That helper passes the configured `pretty_exceptions_show_locals` setting and the internal paths as Rich’s `show_locals` and `suppress` options (`typer/main.py`, lines 77–87; `typer/rich_utils.py`, `get_traceback`, lines 761–776).

Without Rich, Typer formats a standard `TracebackException` and filters internal frames. When `pretty_exceptions_short` is true, those frames are omitted from the stack; when false, they remain but their source lines are blanked (`typer/main.py`, lines 88–108). I could not determine from the returned code how Typer installs or invokes this hook.

rows.question: How does a session combine caller-supplied proxies and TLS verification settings with environment variables and session defaults? Explain when environment values are ignored, how an explicit proxy entry wins, and what a proxy value of None does during merging.
rows.answer:
`merge_environment_settings` first incorporates environment settings when `Session.trust_env` is true; it then merges the resulting request settings with the session’s defaults (`src/requests/sessions.py:750–779`). Environment proxy variables are added with `proxies.setdefault(k, v)`, so a caller-supplied value for the same proxy key wins; the environment only fills keys that are absent (`src/requests/sessions.py:759–762`). If `trust_env` is false, that environment-proxy step and the environment CA-bundle lookup are skipped (`src/requests/sessions.py:757–771`).

The `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE`/`CURL_CA_BUNDLE` setting is consulted only when `verify` is `True` or `None`; an explicit caller value such as a CA-bundle path or `False` prevents the environment value from being used (`src/requests/sessions.py:766–771`). Afterward, request settings take precedence over session defaults: for mappings, the session mapping is copied first and the request mapping updates it (`src/requests/sessions.py:79–80`). A proxy entry whose value is `None` is removed from the merged mapping, so it suppresses that key rather than being passed through as a proxy (`src/requests/sessions.py:82–86`).

def set_blocked(self, name: str) -> None:
        """Block registrations of the given name, unregister if already registered."""

        """Return whether the given plugin name is blocked."""
        return name in self._name2plugin and self._name2plugin[name] is None

rows.question: How does default_if_none choose between a fixed replacement and a factory when an attribute receives None? Explain what happens for non-None input and which invalid configurations fail before conversion.
rows.answer:
`default_if_none` accepts exactly one of `default` or `factory`. If you pass `factory`, it wraps it in an `attrs.Factory`; if `default` itself is an `attrs.Factory`, it uses that factory too. When the attribute value is `None`, the converter calls the factory with no arguments and returns its result; otherwise, it returns the original value unchanged (`src/attr/converters.py:55–111`, `default_if_none`).

Invalid configurations fail when `default_if_none` is set up, before any value conversion: omitting both arguments or passing both raises `TypeError`, and passing an `attrs.Factory` with `takes_self=True` raises `ValueError` (`src/attr/converters.py:55–111`, `default_if_none`).

    def merge_environment_settings(self, url, proxies, stream, verify, cert):
        """
        Check the environment and merge it with some settings.

        :rtype: dict
        """
        # Gather clues from the surrounding environment.
        if self.trust_env:
            # Set environment's proxies.
            no_proxy = proxies.get("no_proxy") if proxies is not None else None
            env_proxies = get_environ_proxies(url, no_proxy=no_proxy)
            for k, v in env_proxies.items():
                proxies.setdefault(k, v)

            # Look for requests environment configuration
            # and be compatible with cURL.
            if verify is True or verify is None:
                verify = (
                    os.environ.get("REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE")
                    or os.environ.get("CURL_CA_BUNDLE")
                    or verify
                )

        # Merge all the kwargs.
        proxies = merge_setting(proxies, self.proxies)
        stream = merge_setting(stream, self.stream)
        verify = merge_setting(verify, self.verify)
        cert = merge_setting(cert, self.cert)

        return {"proxies": proxies, "stream": stream, "verify": verify, "cert": cert}

def merge_setting(request_setting, session_setting, dict_class=OrderedDict):
    """Determines appropriate setting for a given request, taking into account
    the explicit setting on that request, and the setting in the session. If a
    setting is a dictionary, they will be merged together using `dict_class`
    """

    if session_setting is None:
        return request_setting

    if request_setting is None:
        return session_setting

    # Bypass if not a dictionary (e.g. verify)
    if not (
        isinstance(session_setting, Mapping) and isinstance(request_setting, Mapping)
    ):
        return request_setting

    merged_setting = dict_class(to_key_val_list(session_setting))
    merged_setting.update(to_key_val_list(request_setting))

    # Remove keys that are set to None. Extract keys first to avoid altering
    # the dictionary during iteration.
    none_keys = [k for (k, v) in merged_setting.items() if v is None]
    for key in none_keys:
        del merged_setting[key]

    return merged_setting

In `PluginManager.add_hookspecs` (`src/pluggy/_manager.py:249–273`), a matching specification finds the existing `HookCaller` and calls `hc.set_specification(...)`; it then validates each already-registered implementation with `_verify_hook`. `HookCaller.set_specification` (`src/pluggy/_hooks.py:424–436`) assigns a `HookSpec` to `self.spec`, but raises `ValueError` if the caller already has a specification. `_verify_hook` (`src/pluggy/_manager.py:328–379`) compares implementation argument names with the spec’s argument names and raises `PluginValidationError` if an implementation declares an argument the spec lacks.

The code shown assigns the specification **before** validating implementations, so a failed validation does not leave the caller unspecified: its `spec` has already been set. A retry with a corrected specification therefore cannot replace it; `set_specification` rejects a second specification. If the supplied namespace has no matching hook specifications, `add_hookspecs` raises `ValueError` (“did not find any … hooks”). The returned code does not establish whether that no-match case alters any existing caller state.

pairs.winner_answer:
A prepared request is routed by `Session.get_adapter()` when sending: it scans the session’s adapter prefixes in order and returns the first whose prefix matches the URL’s beginning. Matching is case-insensitive for both URL and prefix (`src/requests/sessions.py:787–792`; `tests/test_requests.py:1653–1663`).

`mount()` keeps prefixes sorted by descending length, so among your two custom mounts, `https://api.example.test/v1/` is checked before `https://api.example.test` and wins for URLs beginning with the longer prefix (`src/requests/sessions.py:799–808`). The shorter prefix is just a literal URL prefix—not a host-boundary check—so it can also match strings such as `https://api.example.test.evil/...`. If neither custom prefix matches, the default `https://` adapter handles an HTTPS URL; if no registered prefix matches at all, `get_adapter()` raises `InvalidSchema` (`src/requests/sessions.py:787–792`). Mounting an identical prefix again replaces its adapter in the ordered mapping; it does not create a second competing entry (`src/requests/sessions.py:804–808`).
